articles.title: You could have invented transformers from memory
articles.summary: Transformers can store a potentially unbounded number of memories due to their ability to recall by similarity, as demonstrated by the example of Astra recalling the rules to Dune: Imperium from memory. This recall capability is a key property of good memory stores, which can store a large number of memories before interference with other memories becomes too great. As the number of memories a store can hold increases, the interference-to-signal ratio grows, making it more difficult to recall the stored information. This phenomenon is particularly evident in the development of neural networks, where the capacity of the memory store is a critical factor in determining the performance and efficiency of the model.

articles.title: The Decoherence Trap: When AI slop drowns out the signal in an endless sea of noise
articles.summary: Decoherence grows relative to the rate of change of a system, leading to runaway exponential growth and limiting the rate at which a system can improve outside of its decoherent state. This phenomenon is not new, but the widespread use of AI is currently producing it at a rate that is unsustainable. The good news is that this rules out the specter of runaway recursive self-improvement, but the bad news is that we are barreling toward a different kind of disaster known as Decoherence Collapse, where the accumulation of locally valid but mutually incompatible models within a system leads to a catastrophic collapse of the system's coherence.
